name: Codex CLI
description: Registers Polter's MCP server with OpenAI's Codex CLI and mirrors Polter's skills into ~/.codex/skills/polter-*. Codex keeps TOML at ~/.codex/config.toml under mcp_servers, not the mcpServers every other host uses; the registration goes through `codex mcp` either way.

contains: Would you like to run the following command?
Would you like to make the following edits?
Would you like to grant these permissions?
Would you like to send input to

blocks: Do you trust the contents of this directory?
Set up the Codex agent sandbox

skills.title: Install skills as well
skills.description: yes mirrors Polter's skills into this host's skills directory. Polter's skill_read has to be thought of first; a host's own skills are matched against what the user asked for, which is the whole difference. no registers the MCP server and takes back the polter-* skills an earlier yes installed; skills you wrote yourself are never touched.

approve_tools.title: Let Codex call Polter's tools without asking
approve_tools.description: yes sets default_tools_approval_mode = "approve" on the polter server in ~/.codex/config.toml, and on nothing else. Codex otherwise asks before every call to one of Polter's tools, and a worker nobody is watching stops at the first one, before it can report anything. Your other MCP servers and your global approval policy are not touched. no takes the line back out, and Codex asks again.

rules.title: Write Polter's note into this CLI's rules file
rules.description: yes writes a marked block into the user-level rules file (never a project one) saying that what an agent prints reaches nobody, and pointing at the operating-a-terminal skill. It is there because a skill is matched against what the user asked for and nothing matches "you have just finished a task": on real records, 71 tasks produced 15 done reports. Everything outside the markers is left untouched, and no takes the block back out.

manual_out_of_daemon.title: Let Polter recognise a Codex started by hand
manual_out_of_daemon.description: yes sets daemon_auto_start = false under [features] in ~/.codex/config.toml, and nothing else. Signed in to a ChatGPT account, a Codex you start by typing `codex` runs its session in one background app-server shared by all your terminals, and Polter cannot tell which terminal such a session is in, so it turns its tools off there rather than act as another terminal. With yes, a Codex started by hand no longer uses that shared background server, and Polter recognises it like any other. It changes how Codex runs everywhere on this machine, which is why it is off until you turn it on. A background server that is already running is not stopped and keeps its sessions: the setting takes effect once it has exited (or after you sign in again or restart). Left off: start Codex with `codex --no-daemon`, or from a Polter role, which does so. no takes the line back out; a daemon_auto_start you set yourself is never touched.
